newsitem.title: USA: Venezuela debt prices floating on oil-US investors.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela debt prices floating on oil-US investors.

text.p: The fate of Venezuela's bonds may rest at least for now in the country's oil wealth, as the financial markets watch the government's progress in pursing an agenda for economic reform, U.S. investors said Friday.
Higher global oil prices have helped fuel dramatic gains in Venezuelan debt prices over the past few months, and this upswing has not yet fully run its course.
"Venezuela, in its current fiscal condition, remains a 100 percent oil play," said one portfolio manager at a major U.S. debt fund.
"Provided there is a reasonably good outlook for oil, Venezuela asset prices will look cheap," the portfolio manager said.

Venezuela's bonds, up more than 45 percent so far this year, have surged since President Rafael Caldera's government adopted a plan to steer the country back toward the orthodox economic model. But analysts warned that the runup may not be sustainable if oil prices dip and government reforms falter.
Venezuela's Brady bonds have traded up on prospects that the country can use an estimated $2.5 billion of windfall oil revenues in 1996 to reduce its debt burden.
This effect does not seem likely to diminish any time soon, analysts said.

"Venezuelan Bradies seem fully priced according to fundamentals, but the issue of the debt recovery fund could continue to spark interest in the debt," said Marco Santamaria, vice president at ING Barings.
Venezuelan DCBs VZFLL07=RR, which trade about 550 basis points above U.S. Treasuries, rose 1/4 to a bid price of 82-5/8 On Friday, while the country's FLIRBS VZ6C97=RR gained 3/8 to 83-7/8 bid.

Finance Minister Lus Raul Matos Azocar said Thursday that his country sought to extend its debt maturity profile and said he was studying Mexico's experience of swapping Brady bonds for uncollateralized global paper earlier this year.

Brady bonds, named for former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, were issued by emerging market debtors starting in 1990 to replace defaulted commercial bank borrowings. Swapping Bradies for global bonds would free the U.S. Treasury collateral and remove the stigma of default.
Lasting rewards on the debt front will need to be based in firmer grounding than the oil fields of Orinoco.
A history of unfulfilled pledges to reform has made U.S. investors skeptical of Venezuela's capacity to privatize public firms and trim the state bureaucracy.

The markets will focus on the proposed sale of the state's 49 percent stake in telephone company CANTV, which was planned by the end of November, as a litmus test of the country's commitment to reform, as calls increase for a postponment.

Given resistance from opposision and government lawmakers, resistance to the sale has been rising because of perceived low pricing, although U.S. market players seemed ready to watch and wait before giving reform up for dead.
"You need to give them a chance to get some of these things done," one portfolio manager said. "The trend right now is positive based on statements and on activities."
But analysts noted that the government has few voices that argue unambiguosusly in favor of reform, meaning pension and public sector reform may be a long time coming.
With oil prices riding high, however, investors seemed ready to stick with the belief that Venezuelan Bradies have some energy left.

"I don't see anything really dramatic on the horizon," said the portfolio manager of a small dedicated emerging market fund "Venezuela (debt) should continue for another 50-100 basis points, maybe before the end of the year."
